Here's an interesting post about one of the poems of 14A [Classical Persian poet] RUMI from the internet: "The Guest House": Frequently shared in mindfulness circles, it frames all human emotions—joy, sorrow, and depression—as unexpected visitors to welcome and learn from. Here's the whole poem. I could live by that: This being human is a guest house. Every morning a new arrival. A joy, a depression, a meanness, some momentary awareness comes as an unexpected visitor. Welcome and entertain them all! Even if they’re a crowd of sorrows, who violently sweep your house empty of its furniture, still, treat each guest honorably. He may be clearing you out for some new delight. The dark thought, the shame, the malice, meet them at the door laughing, and invite them in. Be grateful for whoever comes, because each has been sent as a guide from beyond. From--https://www.scottishpoetrylibrary.org.uk/poem/guest-house/

Leftovers: I've been galloping after you all, trying to catch up after spending Sat and Sun enjoying Toronto's lovely autumn and the end of the Jewish holidays. But I did want to reply to one nit from Sunday's puzzle (the grid for which I contemplated in mute delight before actually reading a single clue!) – the argument over the clue at 37A, [One may be teen or false] = IDOL. This is a very mild form of zeugma, the technical term for using one word to mean two different things in one phrase. Here is a page with examples: https://westbraeliterarygroup.com/glossary/zeugma Alas, it doesn't have my favourite from the writer known as "Saki": "The cook was a good cook, as cooks go; and as cooks go, she went."

Then, pleasingly fitting the theme words – a pair of sevens, a pair of sixes, an eight and an 11 – in the grid well, there’s grid-building prowess.

In 1761, Franz Josef Haydn took the second job of his career, as Assistant Music Director of the court orchestra of Prince Paul Anton Esterházy. The old Music Director was, in effect, retired, and so Haydn had to do most of the work, and, when the Director died five years later, was promoted into his position. Paul Anton divided his time between his city home in Vienna, and his country home, Schloss Esterházy, in the rural Hungarian countryside--an even bigger schloss, Esterháza, was built several years later--and the household, including Haydn, followed suit. As a new boss, Haydn was eager to ingratiate himself with his employees, and so, among the first works he wrote for the Esterházy orchestra were three remarkable symphonies--Nos.6-8--themed around time of day. They feature plenty of solos for the principal musicians, in which to show off their chops; if they had been written 200 years later, they would have been called "Concerti for orchestra." Here's No. 7: "NOON," performed by Giardino Armonico: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3jk41uzE89s&list=RD3jk41uzE89s&start_radio=1&t=23s *** Despite his many innovations, Haydn write all that much music in quintuple time: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tT9Eh8wNMkw&list=RDtT9Eh8wNMkw&start_radio=1 *** Nor did he write for female folk trios: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3QMApfa5AUo&list=RD3QMApfa5AUo&start_radio=1 Fun puzzle, fun theme!

Eleven seconds left. Third and four for Arizona on the Giants’ 4-yard line.  Giants up by 6. Field goal means nothing. 

Next play can be a pass or a run. If either results in a touchdown, tie game, Arizona can win on a point-after. 

If it’s an unsuccessful run, time runs out. If it’s an unsuccessful pass, the clock stops and there’s time for one more play, at which point, it can be either a pass or a run. 

So a pass play is the only choice. The Giants knew that. The interception is the only way the Giants stop them then and there. 

The extra six points were just for show and the defender’s stats. Upon the interception, the game was for all intents and purposes over. 

In the older days, the Giants would have been allowed to kick an extra point on top of that. Mercifully, they changed that rule a while back.
